Learning Objectives
Differentiate between shoulder laxity and shoulder instability.
Identify physical examination findings consistent with multidirectional shoulder instability.
Discuss the role of extensive physical therapy in the management of multidirectional shoulder
instability.
Review the goals of surgical management of multidirectional shoulder instability.
Overview and Terminology
Laxity is a physiologic term that refers to passive translation of the humeral head on the
glenoid or over the glenoid rim. Laxity may be pathologic or physiologic.

Glenohumeral instability is a pathologic state in which glenohumeral laxity causes pain,
subluxation, or dislocation.

Overview and Terminology
In discussing multidirectional instability (MDI), differentiating laxity from instability is
important. Laxity refers to passive translation of the humeral head on the glenoid or
over the glenoid rim. Glenohumeral instability refers to the pathologic state in which
glenohumeral laxity causes pain, subluxation, or dislocation. MDI is a specific type of
glenohumeral instability.
Epidemiology
MDI has variable presentations and is difficult to quantify; this has contributed to a paucity of
literature on its epidemiology.
Mean age at presentation is early twenties.

Epidemiology
The variable presentations, changing definitions, and difficultly in categorizing MDI has
contributed to the paucity of literature on the epidemiology. In general, the mean age at
presentation is early twenties.
Classification
Glenohumeral instability represents a spectrum of pathology based on the direction of laxity
(anterior, posterior, or multidirectional) and the underlying cause (traumatic or atraumatic;
(Table 1).
MDI is pathologic glenohumeral laxity with recurrent subluxation or dislocation in more than
one direction.

capsular shift) has been used; however, this descriptor does not accurately apply to all cases of
MDI.


Classification
The most common definition for MDI is shoulder instability characterized by inferior
laxity in addition to anterior and/or posterior laxity. The classic acronym AMBRI has been
used to describe this subset of patients; however, this term does not apply to all cases of
MDI. Patients may have pathologic ligamentous laxity that leads to glenohumeral
instability, but they also may have instability that begins as a specific traumatic event or
instability from repetitive microtrauma.

Anatomy
Glenohumeral stability depends on active and passive restraints.
Passive restraints—The primary passive restraint is the labrum, a cartilaginous ring that
encircles the glenoid, deepening the glenoid fossa and serving as an attachment site for
capsuloligamentous structures. The glenohumeral ligaments form a second important
passive restraint and attach to the glenoid and labrum.
The anterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament (IGHL) is the primary restraint to
anterior translation of the humeral head with the arm in abduction and external rotation.
The posterior band of the IGHL is the primary restraint to posterior translation of the
humeral head with the arm in forward flexion and adduction.
The superior glenohumeral ligament, middle glenohumeral ligament, and coracohumeral
ligament also play important roles in glenohumeral stability.
Active restraints—The rotator cuff muscles, biceps, deltoid, and periscapular muscles are the
main active restraints to glenohumeral instability.
Pathoanatomy/Findings
Capsular laxity: a patulous inferior capsule that contains the anterior and posterior bands of
the IGHL1 (Figure 1)
Rotator interval: functional deficiency
Labral tears: may occur with repeated subluxations or a traumatic event

Evaluation
Patient History
Symptoms range from pain, weakness, ipsilateral paresthesias, popping or clicking of the
shoulder, instability of the shoulder during sleep, difficulty with throwing, and pain when
carrying heavy objects.
Although patients often have bilateral shoulder laxity, most present with unilateral symptoms.
Differential diagnosis includes unidirectional shoulder instability, cervical spine disease,
brachial plexitis, and thoracic outlet syndrome.
Physical Examination
Full shoulder and cervical spine examination

Physical Examination

8/17

The clinical presentation of MDI varies. Many patients report pain and generalized
looseness of the shoulder without frank dislocation. Others report repeated frank
dislocations that arise from minor trauma. Patients with recurrent dislocations may
describe tingling and numbness in their upper extremity in addition to pain. Many
seemingly simple maneuvers, such as pushing open a heavy door or carrying a heavy
object, cause pain, subluxation, or traction paresthesias.
A full shoulder examination, including range of motion and strength testing, should be
performed in addition to specialized tests for instability. Examination of the cervical
spine also is important, especially if the patient presents with neurologic findings in
addition to shoulder complaints. Specialized tests for laxity include the sulcus test, which
evaluates for inferior laxity. Passive external rotation of more than 90° with the arm in
an adducted position also is a sign of hyperlaxity. Anterior and posterior drawer tests
reveal translation of the humeral head on the glenoid. The Gagey hyperabduction test is
used to confirm inferior capsular laxity.
Aside from a shoulder examination, assessment for generalized ligamentous laxity,
which may be a recognized connective tissue disorder, is important. The Beighton score
for hyperlaxity most often is used for this assessment.
Diagnostic Studies
Shoulder radiographs: initial screening tool; often normal in patients with MDI.
MRI
Plain: acceptable for acute injuries in patients with a shoulder effusion
Arthrography: preferred method to evaluate for common soft-tissue pathology, including a
patulous capsule, increased glenohumeral volume, and labral lesions or chondral wear 2
(Figure 5)
CT scan: may be considered if concern exists for bone loss at the humeral head or glenoid
Arthroscopy yields a drive-thru sign, in which the arthroscope easily passes between the
humeral head and the glenoid at the level of the anterior band of the IGHL, indicating
hyperlaxity.

Figure 5 Axial T2-weighted MRI of a right shoulder shows an enlarged posterior capsule (arrow)
and loss of posterior labral height (asterisk) in a patient with multidirectional instability.
(Reproduced from Gaskill TR, Taylor DC, Millett PJ: Management of multidirectional instability of
the shoulder. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2011;19[12]:758-767.)

Diagnostic Studies
MDI usually is a clinical diagnosis; however, imaging studies are helpful. Although
radiographs often appear normal, they may reveal underlying bony anatomy, including
bone loss or abnormal glenoid version or dysplasia. Magnetic resonance arthrography is
the preferred imaging modality to evaluate for joint sequelae of instability, such as labral
lesions or chondral wear; an arthrogram also can help identify findings common in
patients with an MDI diagnosis, such as a patulous capsule and increased glenohumeral
volume. Although not standard, CT may be considered if concern exists for bone loss at
the humeral head or the glenoid or to further define glenoid version or dysplasia.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Extensive physical therapy (6 to 9 months) should be performed before consideration of
surgical management.
SEND FEEDBACK

Physical therapy should primarily focus on evaluation and management of scapulothoracic
dyskinesia. Rotator cuff strengthening and proprioceptive training are secondary focuses.
Motivated patients respond well to appropriate rehabilitation protocols, and establishment of
a maintenance program is essential to maximize long-term success.
Surgical Management
Indications
Pain and instability that interfere with normal or sport-related activity
Failure of extensive nonsurgical management
Ability to comply with postoperative immobilization and rehabilitation
Contraindications
Voluntary instability
Patients who have not attempted physical therapy
Techniques
Surgical management should be individualized to address the anatomic cause of shoulder
instability, including labral repair or bony work.
The mainstay of treatment in patients with MDI involves management of the increased
volume of the joint capsule by addressing the inferior capsule.
Open inferior capsular shift2 (Figure 6)
Deltopectoral approach, subscapularis release or split (Neer capsular shift is a
subscapularis peel off undersurface capsule followed by capsular detachment laterally),
followed by T-capsulotomy with release of the capsule from the humerus
Inferior leaflet—The posterior capsule is advanced inferiorly, and the inferior capsule is
simultaneously advanced anteriorly and superiorly, reducing overall capsular volume.
Superior leaflet: pulled inferiorly and laterally
Rotator interval closure can be performed via this open approach.

Figure 6 Illustrations of a shoulder shows the humeral-based capsular shift described by
Neer and Foster. A, The capsular incision is made between the middle and inferior
glenohumeral ligaments, creating superior (A) and inferior (B) capsular leaflets. B, The
capsular flaps are elevated, and each flap is advanced in the appropriate direction (arrows).
The inferior flap is shifted first. C, The inferior (A) and superior (B) flaps are then sutured.
(Reproduced from Gaskill TR, Taylor DC, Millett PJ: Management of multidirectional
instability of the shoulder. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2011;19[12]:758-767.)
Arthroscopic capsular plication2 (Figure 7)
Advantages of an arthroscopic approach include decreased morbidity, ability to evaluate
all intra-articular structures, and avoidance of subscapularis detachment.
If labral pathology is encountered, anterior or posterior labral repair is indicated.
Plication is completed inferiorly, anteriorly, and posteriorly. Capsular plication begins in
the area of primary instability, decreasing capsular volume as sutures are sequentially
added.
To avoid asymmetric tightening, plication should address the inferior redundancy in a
balanced fashion.

Procedure that results in the most substantial decrease in range of motion in external
rotation with the arm at side.
Can be performed via an open or arthroscopic approach
Thermal capsulorrhaphy
Historical only; no longer recommended because of complications and high failure rates.
Complications
Recurrence (most common)
Subscapularis insufficiency (after open procedure)
Axillary nerve injury
Loss of motion
Postoperative rehabilitation
Shoulder immobilization in brace or sling for at least 4 to 6 weeks postoperatively
Slow progression of external rotation and abduction
Strengthening protocols similar to protocols for the nonsurgical management of MDI

Surgical Management
All patients with MDI should undergo extensive physical therapy (6 to 9 months) before
surgical management is considered. Physical therapy should focus primarily on
evaluation and management of scapulothoracic dyskinesia, with rotator cuff
strengthening and proprioceptive training as secondary focuses. Motivated patients
respond well to appropriate rehabilitation protocols, and establishment of a
maintenance program is essential to maximize long-term success; however, nonsurgical
treatment fails in approximately 20% of patients.
Surgical management should be individualized to address the anatomic causes of
shoulder instability. The most commonly performed procedures for the management of
MDI are open inferior capsular shift and arthroscopic capsular plication.
An open capsular shift, or anteroinferior capsular shift, is performed via a deltopectoral
approach, followed by a subscapular split or tenotomy A T-shaped incision is made
between the inferior and middle glenohumeral ligaments, capsular flaps are elevated off
the humerus, and each of the capsular leaflets are advanced. From the inferior leaflet,

the posterior capsule is advanced inferiorly, and the inferior capsule is simultaneously
advanced anteriorly and superiorly, reducing the posterior capsular redundancy and
eliminating the inferior capsular pouch. The superior leaflet is advanced inferiorly and
laterally over the shifted inferior leaflet.
Arthroscopic pan-capsular plication achieves a similar goal, with the advantage of an
arthroscopic approach that includes decreased morbidity, ability to evaluate all intra-
articular structures, and avoidance of subscapularis detachment. Better visualization
and access allow for potentially more pathology to be managed via a single approach. If
labral pathology is encountered, anterior or posterior labral repair is indicated. Plication
is completed inferiorly, anteriorly, and posteriorly, with capsular plication beginning in
the area of primary instability. Overall, surgeons must proceed from an inferior to
superior fashion, regardless whether beginning anteriorly or posteriorly. As plication
progresses, capsular volume reduction is achieved. To avoid asymmetric tightening,
plication should address inferior redundancy in a balanced fashion.
Rotator interval closure, if indicated, substantially decreases range of motion in external
rotation with the arm at side and can be performed via an open or arthroscopic
approach.
